extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and patentees
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and doctrinal rules used to determine whether an accused device or act infringes a patent (tests of identity, equivalents, acts constituting infringement, intent, and defenses such as experimental use or later patents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Device may infringe despite being a new invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That a device may be an infringement though it constitutes a new invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an accused device is itself a novel invention, it can still infringe if it appropriates the patented invention or its principle (citing California Artificial Stone Paving Co. v. Ferine (1881), Zeun v. Kaldenberg (1883), etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Piracy of the principle is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That if the principle of an invention is pirated there is an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriation of the underlying principle or idea of the patented invention, even if implemented differently, can constitute infringement (see Page v. Ferry (1857)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of ideas despite different appearance is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That identity of ideas, though different in appearance, is infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substance over form: courts look to the idea embodied, not mere outer appearance (Smith v. Higgins (1859), Henderson v. Cleveland Co-operative Stove Co. (1877)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using an essential feature constitutes infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That a device employing an essential feature of the patented invention is an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the accused device uses an essential (material) feature of the claim, it is infringing (Forehand v. Porter (1883), Cannon cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to use patented elements -> infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That wherever the defendants' devices require the use of those patented [elements] there is an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the operation of the accused device necessarily requires use of the patented elements, infringement follows (numerous cases cited: Sayles v. Chicago & Northwestern R.R. Co. (1871), etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of infringement: effects, functions, and modes of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of infringement is whether the defendant uses anything identical in effect, function, and mode of operation: if effects, functions, and modes are identical the ideas must be identical; if any differ substantially there is no identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court applies a three-part practical test: (1) Are the effects produced substantially the same? (2) Are the functions essentially the same? (3) Are the modes of operation the same? If all three are identical, variations in shape, size, arrangement, or materials are unimportant. If any differ substantially, no infringement. (Statements and examples throughout §§ 894-896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference in nature of result shows no infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That difference in the nature of the result shows that there is no infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the end result is of a different nature, courts will find no identity/infringement (May v. County of Fond du Lac (1886)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of result is prima facie evidence of identity of process (when both new)
rubrics_metrics.description: That identity of result is prima facie evidence of identity of process where both are new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When both processes are new and produce the same result, identity of result gives a presumption of identity of process (Pickhardt v. Packard (1884)). See cross-references (§ 117).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement requires identity of function as well as parts
rubrics_metrics.description: That infringement does not exist unless there is identity of function as well as of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require that the accused device replicate the function (not merely some parts) of the patented device; mere similarity of parts is insufficient (Bacine Seeder Co. v. Joliet Wire Check Rower Co. (1886) and related authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Device incapable of performing claimed functions cannot infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: That an article incapable of performing the functions of a patented device cannot be an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the accused article cannot perform the claimed functions, there is no infringement (Railway Register Mfg. Co. v. Broadway & Seventh Ave. R.R. Co. (1887)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity in mode of operation is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: That identity in mode of operation is necessary to infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts emphasize mode of operation: if the mode differs, there may be no infringement (Evory v. Burt (1883) and related cases). See cross-references §§ 285, 886.

rubrics_metrics.name: To obtain the same result by the same mode of operation is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That to obtain the same result by the same mode of operation is infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproducing the same mode that produces the same result is unlawful even if other elements differ (Shaver v. Skinner Mfg. Co. (1887), etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of arrangement may be infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That a change of arrangement may be infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rearranging parts does not necessarily avoid infringement; substantive identity matters (Belle Patent Button Fastener Co. v. Lucas (1887)); see examples where rearrangement held infringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere difference in location of parts will not avoid infringement when function/result/mode identical
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the same result is accomplished, the same function performed, and the mode of operation is the same, a mere difference in the location of parts will not avoid infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spatial shifts that do not change function or mode are immaterial (Kirk v. Du Bois (1887), Byam v. Farr (1852)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere formal modification affecting only quantity of result does not avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That a mere formal modification affecting only the quantity of the result does not avoid infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes that only alter the amount produced, without changing function/mode, remain infringing (Coupe v. Weatherhead (1888); Schmidt v. Freese (1882)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variations in size, form, or degree do not prevent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That variations in size, form, and degree do not prevent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor dimensional or form differences are usually immaterial (Asmus v. Alden (1886); numerous cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent limited to certain forms or materials is infringed only by use of those forms/materials
rubrics_metrics.description: That an invention limited to certain forms is infringed only by the use of those forms; similarly a patent limited to certain materials is infringed only by use of such materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims expressly limit to forms/materials, infringement requires practicing those claimed forms/materials (Wright v. Yuengling (1888); Westem & Wells Mfg. Co. v. Rosenstock (1887)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an equivalent is not infringement when specification excludes it
rubrics_metrics.description: That the use of an equivalent is not an infringement when the specification says it is not within the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent specification expressly disclaims equivalents or states certain equivalents are outside the claim scope, their use may not infringe (Curtia, 260 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference in purpose of use will not prevent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That a difference in the purpose for which the invention is used will not prevent an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using an invention for a different purpose does not avoid liability if function/mode/result remain appropriated (Thompson v. Gilmoreleeve (1888); Stegner v. Blake (1888)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Device may infringe though it can be used in ways the patented device cannot
rubrics_metrics.description: That a device may be an infringement though it can be used in a way in which the patented device cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional capabilities in the accused device do not prevent infringement if it still practices the claimed invention (Yale Lock Mfg. Co. v. Norwich National Bank (1881), Carter v. Baker (1871)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of known device for another (even complex) can be infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That the substitution of one known device for another, though complex, is infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacing claimed elements with known equivalents in order to practice the invention can infringe (Foster v. Moore (1852)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial practice of claimed result may be infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That a device may be an infringement though it only accomplishes in part the result attained by using the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even partial appropriation of the patented result can be infringing (Coupe v. Weatherhead (1883); Sewall v. Jones (1875)). See also §§ 259–271 for diversity of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents and added elements: extra elements may still infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: That a device may be an infringement though additional elements are employed; changes consistent with preserving identity (e.g., consolidation/division of parts, added features) can still appropriate the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding or rearranging parts, or including equivalents that perform the patented function, often preserves infringement under equivalence doctrine (examples: Loercher v. Crandall (1881); Westinghouse Air Brake cases). See §§ 245–258 and notes on equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements can infringe the original patent
rubrics_metrics.description: That an improvement may be an infringement, and an improver may infringe by embodying or using the original invention in his improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An improvement that incorporates the original patented invention (or makes use of it) can infringe even if it adds value or works better (Gray v. James (1817); Boyer v. Coupe (1886); Howes v. McNeal (1878)). However, if the alleged original invention is inoperative, the improver may not infringe by embodying it (Boyer v. Coupe (1886)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity may result from use, not just original construction
rubrics_metrics.description: That identity may result from use as well as from original construction: an instrument which, when employed, develops features that perform the functions of the patented invention becomes identical with it if such result was intended or follows necessarily from its employment; accidental development does not produce identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a device in its practical employment performs the patented functions by the same mode, and that result was intended by maker/user or necessarily follows, courts may impute identity to the original device (Page v. Ferry (1867); many illustrations). But accidental or unintended wear/development that causes similarity does not create identity (§ 896 discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Later patent does not conclusively preclude infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: That identity not controverted by the issue of a later patent for the infringing invention: a later patent does not conclusively establish absence of identity with an earlier patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each patent is prima facie evidence of novelty, but a later patent containing similar subject-matter does not protect its patentee against infringement by the earlier valid patent owner once identity is shown; presumption of diversity can be overcome (Holliday v. Pickhardt (1882); La Baw v. Hawkins (1874); Cantrell v. Wallick (1886)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of act of infringement: making, using, selling (and equivalents)
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringement may be committed either by making, using, or selling the patented invention; these words include every method by which the invention can be made available for the benefit of the infringer, and participation, direct or indirect, that promotes unauthorized manufacture/use/sale renders one a violator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making, using, or selling—even if the maker does not use it—can infringe. Participation (e.g., supplying parts, tools, or sharing profits) can create liability (Haselden v. Ogden (1868); Wells v. Jaques (1874); Vaughn v. East Tennessee R.R. Co. (1877)).

rubrics_metrics.name: No act is infringement unless it affects the patentee's pecuniary interests
rubrics_metrics.description: No act is an infringement unless it affects the pecuniary interests of the owner of the patented invention; purely experimental, scientific, or recreational uses that do not turn to profit may not infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental making/use for curiosity or instruction is generally not infringement unless results are sold or used commercially or to adapt the invention to business (Poppenhusen v. Falke (1861); Frearson v. Loe (1878)). Yet courts may sometimes enjoin experimental uses even absent quantifiable injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession/exposure/advertising not per se infringement but are evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere possession of the patented invention, its exposure for sale, exhibition, or advertising are not, taken alone, acts that disturb the patentee's exclusive rights, though they are strong evidence of underlying acts of making, using, or selling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession for use can be evidence or may be infringement if bought for use; exposure/advertising/exhibition by themselves are insufficient for liability (United Telephone Co. v. London & Globe Telephone Co. (1884); Minter v. Williams (1835)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use/sale/manufacture must relate to the precise invention claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: The acts of manufacture, use, and sale must relate to the precise invention claimed in the patent; using part of the patented invention is not an infringement of a patent covering the whole unless the act appropriates the complete expression of the invention (machine-patent exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using only a portion of a claimed invention (especially when that part is covered by a different patent or disclaimed) is not infringement of the other patent; but machine patents may be infringed where the accused act appropriates the structural law or complete idea of the machine (discussion in § 900 and related notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention of infringer generally immaterial (but may be evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intention with which an act of infringement is performed is immaterial as a general proposition; innocence or ignorance does not avoid liability, though intent may be evidence of infringement in particular contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability attaches regardless of whether the actor intended to violate the patent; courts may, however, consider intent as evidence of willfulness or to show that the accused instrument was constructed/used to produce the patented result (general statement and case examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint and several liability for multiple infringers and profit-sharing as complicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several parties infringe (some by making, others by selling), the infringement is joint and several; sharing in the profits of an infringement or participating in the fruits of infringement can render parties jointly liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgment may be rendered against each infringer even if only one satisfaction is collectable; landlords/others who simply derive incidental benefit are not per se infringers unless arrangement is a cover for participation (Jennings v. Dolan (1887); Starrett v. Athol Machine Co. (1888)).
